teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry M1 V22: Ionic lattices and their properties. Why are ionic solids hard and brittle, and why do they conduct only when their ions can move? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: That structure is called an ionic lattice. It's a giant, regular, three-dimensional pattern of ions, repeating in every direction. In sodium chloride, each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions, and each chloride ion by six sodium ions. There are no separate molecules. The attractions act in every direction at once, and the formula, N a C l, only tells you the ratio of ions, one to one. First, melting. To melt, the ions have to break out of their fixed places, and start moving past each other. But every ion is held by strong attractions to all of its neighbours, so that takes a lot of energy. That's why salt doesn't melt until eight hundred and one degrees Celsius. The charges on the ions matter too. Magnesium oxide is made of magnesium two plus and oxide two minus ions, double the charges in sodium chloride. Bigger charges attract more strongly, so magnesium oxide melts at about two thousand eight hundred and fifty degrees, far higher than salt. It's even used to line furnaces. Smaller ions sit closer together, so they attract more strongly too.

The blow is a coded impact flash; no hammer or hand. Revision 2 (brief 179, root decision 37): halite is brittle, not hard (Mohs about 2 to 2.5), so the hook no longer says it is hard or hard to scratch; it is used for cleavage and brittleness only.
- **Hardness (Revision 2).** The learner question keeps "hard" (root decision 22; v21's chip uses it). Scene 6 explains the cause (ions resist being pushed out of place against strong attractions), names magnesium oxide as a very hard example, and says salt is softer but still breaks rather than bends. No claim that every ionic crystal is scratch-hard.
- **Lattice (site).** Shown as one coded layer growing into a 3 × 3 × 3 cube (rock-salt arrangement), then one Na⁺ with its six Cl⁻ neighbours highlighted. "Ionic network" is named on screen to match the syllabus wording.

Size effect in one sentence with LiF 848 °C and CsI 632 °C as screen tags only (site values). Scene 5 names the trap: dividing Celsius temperatures does not give a ratio of attraction, because 0 °C is not zero energy (site correction 12; the route's "Avoid equating Celsius melting-point ratios with lattice-energy ratios").

- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m1-v23`, "How does molecular shape determine whether bond dipoles cancel?").** Scene 18: salt has no molecules, but water and carbon dioxide do; both have polar bonds (v21), yet only water's molecules have charged ends; the difference is shape. Suggest "the attraction depends on the charges and the distance between ions (Coulomb's law)", without the force formula, or with energy ∝ q₁q₂/r.

- **Board layout (constant):** heading top left; plates or circuit at the left; the lattice or zoom bubble at the right; property chips accumulate in a column at the top right (high melting point, resists denting, brittle, conductivity).
- **Simulations (Revision 2).** (1) The lattice heater: a temperature slider (25 to 900 °C) under the lattice with a readout (52 px); as it rises the ions vibrate harder, and at 801 °C the lattice breaks and the ions slide past each other (scene 3; reused in scene 11). (3) The conductivity tester: a state switch (solid, molten, aqueous) with two readouts, "ions reaching the electrodes" (a running count, 52 px) and the lamp; the count stays at 0 for the solid and climbs for molten and aqueous (scenes 10 to 12).
- **Colour roles (Revision 2, fixed for the whole video):** cations and positive electrodes red; anions and negative electrodes blue; attraction lines grey, amber when named; temperature readouts and the thermometer terracotta; property chips teal; givens strips navy; framed answers dark-ink box with a green tick; crossed slips red strike with a red hand tag; hand tags take the colour of what they mark.
- **Type sizes (Revision 2, 1080p):** the current statement or chain at least 44 px; slider and counter readouts about 52 px; table cells, chips and supporting lines 32 to 36 px; hand tags at least 30 px; nothing a student must read below 26 px. All text above the bottom 12% of the frame.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) NaCl rock-salt structure: face-centred cubic, coordination 6 : 6 (site; standard). The 3 × 3 × 3 cube shown has 14 Cl⁻ and 13 Na⁺ (or the reverse); the 1 : 1 ratio holds for the infinite lattice, which the narration states.
(b) Melting points (site; CRC Handbook in brackets): NaCl 801 °C (800.7); MgO 2852 °C (2825); LiF 848 °C (848.2); CsI 632 °C (632); CaCl₂ 772 °C. Narration rounds MgO to "about two thousand eight hundred and fifty"; attempt 2 uses the site's 2852 °C.
(c) Lattice energies (CRC, approximate): NaCl 787 kJ/mol, MgO about 3800 kJ/mol (about 4.8 to 4.9 times NaCl). Kelvin melting points: 1074 K and 3125 K (ratio 2.9). The Celsius ratio 2852/801 = 3.56 has no physical meaning, and neither ratio equals the lattice-energy ratio; melting point is not proportional to lattice energy. Learner copy: "zero on the Celsius scale isn't zero energy", and "higher charges, stronger attraction, higher melting point".
(d) Hardness and brittleness are described qualitatively (site). Revision 2: halite has Mohs hardness about 2 to 2.5 (soft; a fingernail can just scratch it; https://commonminerals.esci.umn.edu/minerals-g-m/halite), so learner copy never calls salt hard. Periclase (MgO) is about 5.5 to 6 and fused MgO is a refractory, so it is the "very hard" example. Cleavage of halite along {100} planes gives cubic fragments; the plate shows flat faces.
(e) Not all ionic compounds dissolve (CaCO₃, AgCl); solubility is later work. A1 uses calcium chloride, which is very soluble.
(f) Molten NaCl conducts by ion migration; at the electrodes electrolysis produces sodium and chlorine (the Downs cell). Not taught; the narration says only that ions "carry the current".
(g) Conductivity tester: low-voltage (about 3 to 6 V DC) battery supply, carbon (graphite) electrodes, dilute sodium chloride solution; electrodes rinsed between tests. (h) Water's charged ends: v21 taught polar bonds; why water as a whole has charged ends (shape) is v23. Learner copy says "water molecules have slightly charged ends", which v23 then explains; the handoff makes this the next question.
(i) Pronunciations: "aqueous" (AY-kwee-us); "lattice"; "electrode"; "magnesium oxide"; numbers spoken in words.

Main question: *Why are ionic solids hard and brittle, and why do they conduct only when their ions can move?*

The attractions act in every direction at once, and the formula, N a C l, only tells you the ratio of ions, one to one.
